client: I've been really stressed out lately because my final exams are coming up next month, and honestly I feel like I'm already falling behind, especially in statistics. I bombed the last two quizzes in that class and I just can't seem to wrap my head around the material no matter how long I sit with it. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because at the end of the day I still have to go home and actually understand the stuff, you know?
therapist: It makes complete sense that you're feeling overwhelmed — two tough quizzes plus a looming exam is a lot of pressure, and that frustration of sitting with material that won't click is genuinely exhausting. You're right that talking won't magically solve the statistics, but sometimes when we're stressed, our thinking can get in the way of our learning more than the material itself does. I'm curious — when you sit down to study and hit a wall, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind in that moment?

client: Honestly, the first thing that goes through my head is something like "you're too stupid for this" or "everyone else in the class gets it and you're the only one who doesn't." And then I kind of spiral from there, like I start thinking about how if I fail this class it's going to mess up my whole GPA and maybe even my whole future, which sounds dramatic but it feels really real in the moment. By the time I've gone down that road I'm so anxious I can barely even read the words on the page anymore.
therapist: Those thoughts — "I'm too stupid" and "everyone else gets it" — are really common examples of what we call automatic thoughts, and they're worth examining because they feel like facts but they're actually interpretations your stressed mind is generating. It's no wonder you can't absorb statistics when part of your brain is simultaneously running a worst-case-scenario story about your entire future — that's an enormous amount of mental load to carry. I'd love to gently challenge one piece of that: what actual evidence do you have that *everyone else* in the class understands the material, versus that just being a story the anxiety is telling you?

client: I mean, when you put it that way, I guess I don't actually have solid proof that everyone else is breezing through it. But it still feels true, like when I'm sitting in lecture and the professor asks a question and other people raise their hands, it just confirms it for me in that moment. I hear what you're saying about it being an interpretation, but I'm not sure just knowing that is going to make the feeling go away.
therapist: You're making a really sharp observation — knowing something intellectually and *feeling* it differently are two separate things, and CBT isn't about just thinking your way out of emotions overnight. It's also worth noticing that the students raising their hands might be a small handful of the same confident few, while the majority are sitting quietly just like you — your brain is selectively collecting evidence that confirms the story it already believes, which is something we can actually work with. What do you think it might feel like to run a small experiment this week, like asking one classmate how *they're* finding the material, just to test whether the "everyone gets it but me" story holds up?

client: Honestly, the idea of doing that makes me kind of uncomfortable, because what if I ask someone and they actually say they're doing fine and understanding everything? That would just make me feel worse and confirm the thing I'm already afraid of. I also don't really talk to many people in that class, so it's not like I can just casually bring it up without it feeling awkward.
therapist: That hesitation makes a lot of sense, and it actually tells us something really important — your mind is currently set up to interpret almost any outcome as confirmation of the worst, which is a sign of how much anxiety has taken the wheel right now. And honestly, the awkwardness barrier is real too, so we don't have to force that experiment if it doesn't feel right. I'm wondering though — is there a lower-stakes way to test the waters, like checking a class forum or Reddit thread for your course to see if *other* students are expressing confusion about the material?

client: That's actually a little more manageable than talking to someone face to face, so I could probably do that. But I guess part of me is worried that even if I find a bunch of posts from people saying they're confused too, I'll just tell myself "yeah but they're probably still doing better than me" and dismiss it. It's like you said, my brain seems really good at finding ways to keep the bad story going no matter what.
therapist: You've just made a really profound observation about yourself — recognizing that your mind has a habit of moving the goalposts to keep the negative story alive is actually a huge insight, and that kind of self-awareness is exactly what starts to loosen anxiety's grip over time. It sounds like the core belief underneath all of this might be something deeper than just "I don't understand statistics" — more like "I'm fundamentally not capable," and that belief is working hard to protect itself from any evidence that contradicts it. What do you think that belief might be protecting you from — like, what would it mean for you if it turned out you *weren't* as behind as you fear?

client: That's a weird question to sit with, because my gut reaction is like... relief, I guess, but also almost a kind of pressure? Like if I'm not actually as far behind as I think, then I don't have an excuse anymore and I just have to perform, and what if I try my hardest and still fail anyway. I think that's scarier to me than just assuming I'm already doomed, because at least then I'm not really putting myself on the line.
therapist: What you just shared is incredibly courageous and honest — you've identified something really core here, which is that "I'm already doomed" actually feels *safer* than trying, because trying means risking genuine failure and that feels much more exposing. That's not a personal flaw, it's a very human way of protecting yourself from pain, but it also means the anxiety is costing you something real — the chance to find out what you're actually capable of. I'm curious, has there been a time in your life where you took that risk of genuinely trying at something difficult, and what happened?

client: There was this one time in high school where I really struggled with chemistry and I actually put in a ton of effort studying for the final, like genuinely tried instead of just going through the motions, and I ended up passing with a decent grade. But I think I've kind of buried that memory because it feels different now, like college is higher stakes and one good grade back then doesn't really prove anything about what I can do now. I guess I'm not sure how much weight to give that experience when everything feels so much more serious these days.
therapist: That memory is actually really significant — your brain has been so focused on collecting evidence that you can't do this that it's been actively minimizing a moment where you faced something hard, genuinely tried, and came through. You're right that college feels higher stakes, but the core of what that chemistry experience shows isn't "I can ace easy things" — it's "when I actually engage instead of protecting myself, I'm more capable than I give myself credit for." I wonder, what might it look like to bring even a fraction of that same genuine effort to statistics — not to guarantee a perfect outcome, but just as an experiment in showing up for yourself?

client: I think what makes that hard is that in high school I didn't fully realize how much was riding on it, so I could just focus on the work without all this noise in my head. Now every time I sit down to study statistics I'm already thinking about grades and GPA and what it means about me as a person, and I don't know how to just turn that off and be present with the material the way I was back then. I want to try, I really do, but I'm not sure how to get out of my own way long enough to actually do it.
therapist: What you're describing — that the noise itself is the obstacle more than the statistics — is such a key insight, and it points to something really practical we can work with. One small thing worth experimenting with is giving yourself a very short, bounded study block, like 20 minutes, where your only job is to engage with one problem, not to fix your GPA or prove anything about yourself — almost like tricking your brain into that high school mindset by shrinking the stakes down to just *this one problem, right now*. What do you think would happen if you tried that kind of focused, low-pressure block just once this week and noticed what came up?

client: I think I could probably manage 20 minutes, that doesn't sound as overwhelming as what I usually try to do, which is like sit down for hours and then burn out after 30 minutes anyway. But I'm a little worried that even in those 20 minutes the anxious thoughts are still going to creep in, like I'll be looking at a statistics problem and suddenly I'm thinking about my GPA again and the whole thing falls apart. Is there something I'm supposed to do when that happens, or do I just try to push through it?
therapist: The anxious thoughts will almost certainly show up — and the goal isn't to push them away or power through, but to practice noticing them without letting them drive, almost like seeing a notification pop up on your phone and choosing not to open it right now. When a thought like "this affects my GPA" appears, you can try briefly acknowledging it — something like "there's that thought again" — and then gently redirecting your attention back to just the problem in front of you, which over time actually weakens the thought's grip more than fighting it does. What do you think feels more doable to you — trying to suppress those thoughts when they come up, or practicing that kind of "notice and return" approach?

client: The "notice and return" thing sounds more realistic than trying to suppress them, because I've already figured out that trying to force the thoughts out just makes them louder. I guess my worry is that in the moment it's going to feel really mechanical, like I'll be saying "there's that thought again" but still feel completely hijacked by the anxiety underneath it. I'm willing to try it, but I just don't want to feel like I'm failing at the technique on top of already feeling like I'm failing at statistics.
therapist: That concern is so valid, and I want to be really clear: there is no way to fail at this technique, because even noticing that you got hijacked *after the fact* is still practicing the skill — the noticing itself is the work, not perfectly staying calm in the moment. Think of it less like a switch you flip and more like a muscle you're just beginning to build, so feeling swept up by anxiety sometimes isn't a sign it's not working, it's just part of the early stages of learning. How would it feel to go into that 20-minute session this week with the explicit expectation that the anxious thoughts *will* show up, so that when they do it feels like "yep, there it is, just like Luna said" rather than evidence that you're failing?
